paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: projectile motion
paragraphs.meaning: A projectile moves because two independent motions happen at once: constant velocity horizontally and constant acceleration downward. They share the same time, which is why the vertical motion alone decides how long the flight lasts. Time of flight is 2u sin θ / g and range is u² sin 2θ / g, both measured from the same launch height.

words.meaning: The total time a projectile stays in the air.
words.breakdown: T = 2u sin θ / g on level ground. It depends only on the vertical component of the launch velocity.
words.trap: Horizontal speed does not change the time of flight. A bullet fired horizontally and one dropped from the same height land together.

words.meaning: The horizontal distance covered before the projectile returns to launch height.
words.breakdown: R = u² sin 2θ / g, largest at 45 degrees.
words.trap: Maximum range is at 45 degrees only on level ground with no air resistance. A launch from a height peaks at a lower angle.

words.meaning: The path followed by the projectile, a parabola when only gravity acts.
words.breakdown: y = x tan θ - gx² / (2u² cos²θ).
words.trap: The parabola is a shape, not a force. Nothing pushes the projectile along the curve.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M24 116h276'/><path class='d-accent' d='M44 116c30-70 70-96 110-78 44 20 60 78 92 78'/><path class='d-guide' d='M154 116V56'/><text class='d-label' x='120' y='132'>apex: vertical speed zero</text><text class='d-label' x='40' y='38'>same clock for both motions</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A parabolic path with a vertical guide at the highest point where the vertical velocity is zero.
paragraphs.hook: Fire a bullet horizontally and drop one at the same moment: they hit the ground together.
paragraphs.exam_note: Two angles giving the same range add to 90 degrees. Questions use this instead of solving the quadratic.
paragraphs.trap: At the highest point the velocity is not zero, only its vertical component. The horizontal component keeps going.

recall.q: A projectile is launched at 30 degrees and another at 60 degrees with the same speed. Their ranges are
recall.why: Range depends on sin 2θ, and sin 60 equals sin 120, so complementary angles give the same range.

recall.q: At the highest point of its path, a projectile has
recall.why: The vertical component is zero at the apex, but the horizontal component is unchanged, so velocity is horizontal, not zero.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the formulae as printed in your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: relative velocity
paragraphs.meaning: The velocity of A as seen from B is the velocity of A minus the velocity of B, subtracted as vectors, not as magnitudes. That is why rain falling straight down appears slanted when you run, and why two cars at 60 km/h in opposite directions close at 120 km/h. Drawing the subtraction triangle answers most questions faster than the algebra.

words.meaning: The velocity of one body measured in the frame of another.
words.breakdown: v(A relative to B) = v(A) - v(B), vector subtraction.
words.trap: Never subtract speeds unless the motions are along the same line. At an angle, the magnitudes do not simply subtract.

words.meaning: The body and coordinate system against which motion is measured.
words.breakdown: Changing the frame adds a constant velocity to everything and leaves relative motion unchanged.
words.trap: A frame moving at constant velocity is inertial, so the laws of motion still hold in it. Only accelerating frames need pseudo forces.

words.meaning: The single vector that replaces two or more vectors.
words.breakdown: For perpendicular vectors, magnitude is the square root of the sum of squares.
words.trap: The resultant of two equal vectors is not their sum unless they point the same way.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M40 40v70'/><path class='d-accent' d='M40 40l90 40'/><path class='d-guide' d='M130 80l0-40'/><text class='d-label' x='48' y='34'>rain, straight down</text><text class='d-label' x='48' y='100'>what you see while running</text><circle class='d-fill' cx='196' cy='74' r='4'/><path class='d-muted' d='M196 74l20-10M190 60l-14 22'/><text class='d-label' x='232' y='66'>add the runner's</text><text class='d-label' x='232' y='84'>velocity, get a slant</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A vertical rain vector combined with a horizontal running vector to give a slanted apparent direction.
paragraphs.hook: The rain is not leaning. You are the one moving sideways.
paragraphs.exam_note: Typical question: rain falls at 4 m/s and you walk at 3 m/s, find the angle the umbrella should make. The answer is arctan(3/4) from the vertical.
paragraphs.trap: The apparent speed is the magnitude of the difference vector, not the difference of magnitudes. 4 and 3 give 5, not 1.

recall.q: Rain falls vertically at 4 m/s. A person walks at 3 m/s. The rain appears to fall at
recall.why: The relative velocity is the vector difference, so its magnitude is the square root of 4 squared plus 3 squared, which is 5 m/s, tilted.

recall.q: Two trains of length 100 m each pass in opposite directions at 10 m/s each. The time to cross is
recall.why: Relative speed is 20 m/s and the total length to clear is 200 m, so the time is 10 s.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the rain example numbers against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: crossing a river
paragraphs.key_phrase: shortest time or shortest path, not both
paragraphs.meaning: To cross a river in the shortest time, aim the boat straight across, and the current carries you downstream while you cross. To land directly opposite, you must aim upstream so that the current is cancelled, which takes longer. The two goals conflict because the crossing depends only on the component of your velocity across the river.

words.meaning: How far downstream the current carries you during the crossing.
words.breakdown: Drift equals the current speed multiplied by the crossing time.
words.trap: Aiming straight across gives shortest time but maximum drift. You cannot avoid drift and save time at once.

words.meaning: The part of a vector along a chosen direction.
words.breakdown: Only the component perpendicular to the bank shortens the crossing time.
words.trap: The boat's speed in still water is not its speed across the ground. The current adds to it as a vector.

words.meaning: The boat's actual velocity relative to the bank.
words.breakdown: It is the vector sum of the boat's velocity in still water and the river's velocity.
words.trap: If the current is faster than the boat, landing directly opposite is impossible, no matter which way you aim.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M20 30h280M20 120h280'/><path class='d-accent' d='M60 120V56'/><path class='d-muted' d='M60 120l70 0'/><text class='d-label' x='66' y='48'>shortest time</text><text class='d-label' x='134' y='136'>drift</text><path class='d-accent' d='M226 118l-24-58'/><text class='d-label' x='186' y='48'>aim upstream</text><text class='d-label' x='196' y='136'>lands opposite</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: Two crossings side by side: one straight across that drifts downstream, one aimed upstream that lands opposite.
paragraphs.hook: Aiming straight across is the fastest way over and the worst way to arrive where you meant to.
paragraphs.exam_note: Shortest time is width divided by boat speed. Shortest path is width divided by the square root of boat speed squared minus current speed squared.
paragraphs.trap: Do not use the boat speed in still water as the crossing speed when the boat is aimed upstream. Only its component across counts.

recall.q: To cross a river in the shortest time, the boat should be aimed
recall.why: The whole boat speed then points across the river, so the crossing time is the width divided by that speed, which is the smallest possible.

recall.q: If the river current is faster than the boat's speed in still water, landing directly opposite is
recall.why: Cancelling the current needs an upstream component bigger than the current, which the boat cannot supply when it is slower.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the worked example against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 3, Motion in a Plane: uniform circular motion
paragraphs.meaning: In uniform circular motion the speed stays the same while the direction changes every instant, so the velocity changes and there is an acceleration pointing at the centre. Its size is v²/r, or ω²r. Remove the inward force and the body does not fly outward; it leaves along the tangent, which is what a stone does when the string snaps.

words.meaning: The acceleration directed towards the centre of a circular path.
words.breakdown: a = v²/r = ω²r. It changes direction, not speed.
words.trap: Centripetal force is not an extra force. It is the name for whatever force happens to point inward, such as tension or gravity.

words.meaning: The rate of change of angle, ω = θ/t, in radians per second.
words.breakdown: v = ωr relates the linear and angular speeds.
words.trap: Angular velocity is the same for all points on a rigid rotating body, but linear speed grows with r.

words.meaning: A pseudo force that appears only in a rotating frame, pointing away from the centre.
words.breakdown: It has no counterpart in the ground frame, where the real force points inward.
words.trap: There is no outward force on a car turning a corner. The friction points inward; your body's inertia makes you feel pushed outward.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><circle class='d-line' cx='130' cy='76' r='44'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='174' cy='76' r='5'/><path class='d-accent' d='M174 76l-26 0M152 70l-6 6 6 6'/><path class='d-muted' d='M174 76v-30M174 46l-5 8M174 46l5 8'/><text class='d-label' x='182' y='44'>motion</text><text class='d-label' x='100' y='50'>force to centre</text><text class='d-label' x='182' y='96'>cut the string:</text><text class='d-label' x='182' y='112'>the stone leaves along the tangent</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A body on a circular path with the inward acceleration arrow and a tangent showing where it goes if released.
paragraphs.hook: The string does not hold the stone out. It keeps pulling it away from the straight line it wants.
paragraphs.exam_note: Questions use a = v²/r with tension, friction or gravity as the inward force. Setting the inward force equal to mv²/r is the whole method.
paragraphs.trap: Writing centripetal force as a separate arrow added to the diagram leads to double counting. It is the net inward force.

recall.q: A body moves on a circle at constant speed. Its acceleration
recall.why: The speed is constant but the direction changes, and the change in velocity always points towards the centre.

recall.q: Two points on a rotating disc, one at twice the radius, have linear speeds in the ratio
recall.why: v = ωr with the same ω, so the point at twice the radius moves twice as fast.
